reference.source: Resnick's Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: A rare sclerosing bone dysplasia combining generalised osteosclerosis with flattened vertebral bodies (platyspondyly) and, characteristically, sclerosis that spares or under-modifies the metaphyses
Presents in childhood with short stature, fractures despite dense bone, and sometimes developmental delay
Recognised causes include recessive variants in SLC29A3 and in TNFRSF11A, reflecting genetic heterogeneity within the phenotype
The paradox of dense yet fragile bone reflects disordered bone modelling and impaired resorption rather than simply increased mass
Radiographs typically show a dense skull base, platyspondyly and abnormal metaphyseal modelling of the long bones
Some individuals develop cranial-nerve compromise, including visual or hearing impairment, from skull-base sclerosis, and dental anomalies may occur
Management is supportive and orthopaedic, with fracture care, monitoring for cranial-nerve compression and decompression of affected foramina where indicated
reference.pathophysiology: Dysosteosclerosis is a heterogeneous recessive disorder of bone modelling in which osteoclast-mediated resorption and the normal shaping of bone are disturbed, producing generalised osteosclerosis together with distinctive platyspondyly. Variants in SLC29A3, a nucleoside transporter, and in TNFRSF11A (RANK), central to osteoclast differentiation, have both been implicated, indicating that different molecular lesions converge on impaired bone remodelling. The accumulated bone is abnormally dense yet mechanically defective, explaining the coexistence of sclerosis and fracture susceptibility. Sclerosis of the skull base can narrow neural foramina and compromise cranial nerves, while the vertebral flattening and abnormal metaphyseal modelling reflect the same failure of orderly bone turnover.
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey demonstrating osteosclerosis, platyspondyly and abnormal metaphyseal modelling
Skull imaging to assess skull-base sclerosis and foraminal narrowing
Cranial-nerve assessment including audiometry and visual evaluation
Bone biochemistry and, where relevant, markers of bone turnover to characterise the disorder
Molecular genetic testing including SLC29A3 and TNFRSF11A
Dental review for associated dental anomalies
redFlags: Progressive visual or hearing loss suggesting cranial-nerve foraminal compression
Recurrent fractures despite dense bone indicating significant bone fragility
Neurological signs of brainstem or spinal cord compromise
Features of marrow failure suggesting an osteopetrosis-like process
reference.prognosis: The prognosis varies with severity and genetic subtype, ranging from relatively mild disease with orthopaedic morbidity to more severe presentations complicated by cranial-nerve deficits and recurrent fractures.
pitfalls: Assuming dense bone is strong bone and underestimating the fracture risk
Confusing the disorder with osteopetrosis and missing the characteristic platyspondyly
Neglecting surveillance for cranial-nerve compression from skull-base sclerosis
Not pursuing molecular testing given the genetic heterogeneity and implications for counselling
references: Resnick's Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders
management: Manage fractures orthopaedically with careful fixation, recognising that the dense bone is mechanically defective and prone to failure
Undertake regular cranial-nerve surveillance with audiometry and visual assessment to detect skull-base foraminal compression early
Offer surgical decompression of narrowed neural foramina to relieve or prevent cranial-nerve compromise
Provide physiotherapy, mobility support and fall-prevention measures to reduce fracture risk
Arrange dental review and management of associated dental anomalies
Offer genetic counselling and family testing given recessive SLC29A3 and TNFRSF11A inheritance
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across metabolic bone, orthopaedics, otolaryngology, ophthalmology and clinical genetics
Escalate promptly for new visual or hearing loss suggesting progressive foraminal narrowing
